Meeting header:
Date: 2027-09-30
Start: 15:00 PDT
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Alex Navarro (Redwood AE), Maria Chen (Redwood SE), Ethan Brooks (Redwood SE), Sofia Patel (Redwood CSM), Jordan Lee (Riptide CTO), Samir Patel (Riptide Lead Infra), Nora Kim (Riptide Product), Liam O'Rourke (Riptide DevOps)

Auto Summary (auto-generated, rough):
Riptide is evaluating Redwood for a production streaming assistant. Main asks: p95 < 300ms for short responses, sustained concurrency ~200 users, peak bursts to 600 concurrent streams, want deterministic p95 and predictable cost. Discussed Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private tradeoffs: Hosted fastest to try, Dedicated for committed throughput, Private for data residency and compliance. Plan: run token/sec benchmarks and streaming p95 tests with representative prompts, try caching + batching configs, consider 8 bit quantized model variant for cost. Next: Redwood to send benchmark template and pilot config; Riptide to share prompts and infra details.

Topics:
- p95 targets and how Redwood measures p95 for streaming
- concurrency math: sessions -> concurrent streams -> tokens/sec
- fallback strategies and graceful degradation (model variants, regional fallback)
- security/compliance: SSO/SAML, SOC2 type II, KMS/HSM, VPC peering
- benchmark plan: sample script, metrics to collect, expected runtime

Action items (recorded): see action_items field above.

Transcript body (timestamps approximate, transcription imperfect):
[00:00] Alex Navarro: hey everyone, thanks for joining, i'm alex with redwood inference, with maria and ethan on the line. how are you all?
[00:06] Jordan Lee: yeah good, thanks. just to kick off, we are here because we need predictable streaming latency, basically p95 for user-facing assistant flows. we were seeing some weird spikes with our current vendor.
[00:16] Maria Chen: thanks jordan, can you quantify "predictable"? like what numbers are you trying to hit for p95 and for what prompt lengths?
[00:23] Jordan Lee: for short prompts — under 64 tokens — we want p95 token completion under 300 ms end-to-end. for multi-turn (200-400 tokens) p95 ideally under 800 ms, and during normal load concurrency ~200 concurrent streams, but we need burst tolerance up to 600 for marketing events.
[00:38] Samir Patel: and to add on infra side, we run in GCP europe-west1 for prod, also have an on-prem lab we can use for a private pilot. data residency is a hard requirement for certain customers so private is important later.
[00:49] Ethan Brooks: understood. quick clarify — are those p95 numbers measured at client side or at model decode? that distinction matters because network + routing adds a bunch.
[00:58] Nora Kim: client side, yes. users see the whole lag. we also stream tokens to the client so p95 for first token is important.
[01:06] Maria Chen: okay great. so our measurement methodology should capture first-token latency and end-to-end p95. we usually instrument both: model latency, RTX decode time, and network hop. our hosted offering gives you metrics out of the box, dedicated lets us reserve capacity for steady throughput, and private gives you the most deterministic network path.
[01:22] Liam O'Rourke: on the topic of streaming, do you support continuous batching with small batch sizes? our workloads are chatty — many short messages.
[01:29] Maria Chen: yes, the runtime is optimized for continuous batching. we adaptively form micro-batches, and we also support prefix / KV cache to avoid repeating past context. small batches do trade off throughput efficiency vs latency. we can tune the batching window.
[01:39] Jordan Lee: you mentioned caching — can you explain typical hit rates and how that affects p95 in tail cases? also, can the cache be pinned per-tenant for privacy?
[01:47] Maria Chen: typical hit-rate depends on your prompt reuse, but for assistant scenarios we've seen 20-40% KV cache hits which reduce tokens/sec and latency. cache can be tenant-isolated in dedicated/private; hosted supports strong isolation but customers with strict compliance usually pick private so they control cache lifecycle and encryption keys.
[02:02] Samir Patel: speaking of keys, we use CloudKMS and HSM for some secrets. can you integrate so keys never leave our control?
[02:09] Alex Navarro: yes, private offering supports KMS/HSM integration, bring-your-own-key, and we provide audit logs for every inference. hosted supports envelope encryption and we can discuss a KMS integration for enterprise plans.
[02:18] Jordan Lee: good. what about throughput math — how do you translate concurrent sessions to required GPU capacity? we need a model to estimate cost because our finance team wants worst-case dollars.
[02:27] Ethan Brooks: great question. we usually build a throughput model: define average tokens per request, tokens/sec per GPU for your model variant, micro-batch efficiency curve, and expected concurrency. from that we supply a recommended cluster size for dedicated or a pilot plan for hosted with burst. we can share a spreadsheet.
[02:40] Nora Kim: can you give a back-of-envelope for say 200 concurrent streams, avg 20 tokens per response, with a model that does 5k tokens/sec on a single GPU?
[02:49] Maria Chen: rough calc: 200 streams * 20 tokens = 4k tokens per full-response window. If your users average 1 response/sec, that's 4k tokens/sec. at 5k tokens/sec per GPU, you need ~1 GPU with small safety margin; but micro-batching inefficiencies and burst Headroom push us to recommend 2x capacity — so 2 GPUs for safety, or use dedicated with autoscale to handle bursts to 600.
[03:07] Samir Patel: hmm interesting. what's the p95 impact if we enable 8-bit quantization for cost-savings? we've seen some quality drift.
[03:15] Maria Chen: quantization reduces memory and can increase throughput; quality impact depends on model and prompts. our Optimize toolkit can run a small eval set (your prompts) to show token-level differences. for many tasks 8-bit is fine; for hallucination-sensitive or long-context tasks we recommend mixed approach — e.g., quantized for background tasks, full-precision for critical path.
[03:33] Jordan Lee: what about fallbacks — if dedicated cluster is saturated, can requests fall back to hosted regionally? we need a transparent behavior for SLA.
[03:41] Alex Navarro: yes, smart routing supports tiered fallback. you can set policy: try dedicated, if latency jumps or capacity lacks, fallback to hosted model variant. we also do automatic model-variant fallbacks (smaller model) to preserve correctness. We'll include recommended policies in the pilot config.
[03:55] Liam O'Rourke: network topology — for private deployment we need details on VPC peering and bandwidth requirements. any guidance?
[04:01] Ethan Brooks: for streaming you need low jitter; we recommend colocating inference cluster near your app tier or use private link. We'll provide a checklist: peering, NAT choices, MTU tuning, and egress requirements.
[04:12] Nora Kim: okay, let's talk benchmarking — what scripts do you need from us?
[04:17] Maria Chen: ideally a representative prompt set, concurrency profile over time (normal and burst), and any multi-turn patterns. we'll provide a script that simulates streaming clients to capture first-token and p95 across percentile buckets.
[04:28] Jordan Lee: timeline — if we start pilot next week, how long to get meaningful p95 numbers?
[04:33] Maria Chen: for baseline single-model runs, 24-48 hours of steady-state runs plus a couple of synthetic bursts to exercise autoscale is enough. For multi-variant configs and quantization evals, 5-7 days to iterate and validate.
[04:44] Samir Patel: audit/compliance — SOC2 and SAML support? we need SSO for our engineers and audit trails for every call.
[04:50] Alex Navarro: yes we have SOC 2 Type II compliance. We support SAML/SSO with Okta and can forward audit logs to your SIEM. For private, you control KMS and logs. We'll attach the security pack in the follow-up email.
[04:59] Jordan Lee: ok. price question: if we go dedicated reserved monthly, what's the cost delta vs hosted?
[05:04] Alex Navarro: dedicated is negotiated based on committed GPUs and usage; per-GPU unit cost is lower when reserved. Hosted is pay-as-you-go and easier to start. We'll provide a cost model in the spreadsheet: committed vs on-demand plus estimated token costs.
[05:16] Nora Kim: any gotchas we should be aware of? throttles, p95 outliers, cold starts?
[05:20] Maria Chen: cold-starts only matter if you spin down nodes aggressively; for streaming we recommend keep-alive instances during predictable windows. Throttles are controlled by rate-limits; we can surface token- and route-level SLOs in the console and automatically open canaries.
[05:33] Jordan Lee: do you have customers who run entirely private on-prem for strict data residency? curious about reference architecture.
[05:38] Alex Navarro: yes, several regulated customers run private (on-prem) with a customer-managed control plane and Redwood runtime inside their network. We'll redaction an architecture doc and reference call if you'd like.
[05:47] Samir Patel: last question — we'll need a POC success criteria. what would you recommend?
[05:52] Maria Chen: recommend: 1) First-token p95 < your target (300 ms) across representative prompts during steady-state at 200 concurrency; 2) successful burst handling to 600 with p95 < 1s; 3) quality parity for quantized variant within X BLEU/ROUGE or human evaluation; 4) integration with SSO/KMS. If we hit those, move to reserved capacity or private.
[06:14] Jordan Lee: sounds good. next steps recap?
[06:18] Alex Navarro: I'll send benchmark template and security pack. Maria will propose pilot config and cost. Samir will share infra details. Jordan will share the prompt set. We'll aim to start pilot first week of October.
[06:30] Nora Kim: thanks everyone.
[06:31] Alex Navarro: thanks, talk soon.

End of call.
